display: ## The Core Fix: Key Pooling Through Your LiteLLM Proxy

Since you're already running a local reverse proxy (LiteLLM) between Claude Code and your GLM API, the "upgrade" isn't really an upgrade to the proxy itself — it's configuring LiteLLM's built-in **load balancing/router** feature to pool multiple GLM API keys behind a single model name, so requests get distributed across all your keys instead of hammering one free-tier key and hitting its rate/latency ceiling.[1][2]

iteLLM treats multiple `model_list` entries with the same `model_name` but different `api_key` values as interchangeable backends and automatically spreads traffic across them. So instead of exposing "GLM-5.2 via key A" as your only route, you register the same model 3–5 times, once per free key/account, and let LiteLLM's router pick the next available one on every request.[3][4]
ttern used in a working "Claude Code via LiteLLM" project that pools multiple keys per provider specifically to double effective rate limits and reduce stalls when one key throttles.[5]

r your goal of reducing latency specifically, `latency-based-routing` is the right strategy — it tracks response times per key and increasingly favors whichever key/account is responding fastest at that moment, rather than blindly round-robining. `simple-shuffle` (the LiteLLM default) is fine for basic distribution but doesn't optimize for speed the way latency-based routing does.[2][6][1]
tegy | What it optimizes | Best fit for your case |
| Even distribution | General baseline, not speed-focused [1] |
Fewest in-flight requests | Good if you're firing many concurrent requests [2] |
atency-based-routing | Fastest-responding key wins more traffic | Best for your "make it faster" goal [5][6] |
outing-v2 | Global RPM/TPM tracking via Redis | Best if you want to strictly avoid ever tripping rate limits across many keys/nodes [6] |
## Failover and Cooldowns (Prevents Slow/Dead Keys From Blocking You)

t `allowed_fails` and `cooldown_time` so that if one free key/account gets rate-limited or errors out, LiteLLM automatically benches it for a set period (e.g. 60s) and routes around it instead of retrying a dead key and adding latency. Pair this with `num_retries: 2` so a single failed call auto-retries on a different key within the same request rather than surfacing an error to Claude Code.[4][2]
## Caching to Cut Redundant Calls (Your Stated Priority)

e you said the goal is caching/streaming optimization rather than paid upgrades, LiteLLM also supports a response cache layer (Redis or in-memory) that you can enable in the same config to short-circuit repeated/identical prompts, which reduces both load on your free keys and perceived latency for repeat queries — add this alongside the router settings rather than as a separate system.

om the start rather than waiting until you hit limits, and use a predictable naming convention like `GLM_API_KEY_1`, `_2`, `_3` in your `.env` so the config stays readable as you add more free accounts. Monitor per-key usage and error rates via LiteLLM's built-in `/ui` dashboard to see which of your free accounts is getting hammered and whether you need to add a 4th.[3]

r LiteLLM proxy config is updated with pooled keys, nothing changes on the Claude Code side — it still just points at `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4000` (or wherever your proxy runs) and requests `glm-5.2`; LiteLLM handles the key rotation transparently underneath. If you're using CC Switch or Zhipu's native `api.z.ai` endpoint directly instead of a self-hosted proxy, note that pooling only works through LiteLLM (or a similar self-hosted proxy) — Zhipu's native endpoint doesn't do multi-key balancing on its own.[7][8][9][5]

Why NIM feels slow on your setupThe free nvapi- key is rate-limited at roughly 40 RPM at the account level, not per model, so if your app calls multiple models (or multiple agent steps) concurrently, they all draw from the same shared bucket and you exhaust it in seconds. Once you exceed the cap, NIM returns HTTP 429 and honors a Retry-After header, so any perceived "slowness" is often your client silently retrying/backing off rather than NIM itself being sluggish.[1][4]
